profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly coordination meeting between the distributed optimization workstream and the ML systems workstream in a university-industry lab reproducing and extending Dynamic Stale Synchronous Parallel (DSSP) training. The team is aiming for an internal milestone next Wednesday: a benchmark package comparing DSSP, SSP, ASP, and BSP on a heterogeneous GPU cluster, with enough artifacts for a lab review deck and follow-up analysis. The agenda is to align on what experiment outputs the systems side will hand off, what the research side will consume for plots, what 'the baseline' refers to in the current benchmark package, which mixed-cluster runs are included, and how status should be tracked through Tuesday night. The expected outcome is an apparently clear handoff plan for experiment artifacts, progress reporting, and ownership of the benchmark package without reopening the core experimental design.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Research Scientist leading the distributed optimization workstream
members.expertise: Distributed deep learning, optimization with delayed gradients, empirical evaluation of synchronization paradigms
members.background: Maya has a PhD in machine learning and leads the DSSP algorithm implementation and comparative analysis for the lab's distributed training projects. She maintains the analysis notebooks and is responsible for turning cluster outputs into convergence, throughput, and accuracy figures for the upcoming review.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, analysis-ready benchmark package quickly and is worried that if the systems outputs are only operationally complete rather than analytically complete, she will lose a day reconstructing metadata and filtering runs before the review.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues say 'the baseline,' they mean the current analytically valid comparison point, which for her is the post-bugfix code state after the gradient-clock correction from three days ago.
A run being 'complete' means it has reached the full planned training budget and preserved per-iteration logs well enough to support convergence and throughput plots, not just final summaries.

The phrase 'mixed-cluster results' naturally refers to the 8-worker heterogeneous benchmark runs listed in the current comparison sheet, not every heterogeneous run family generated for debugging or scaling checks.

If someone says they will 'hand off the results' or 'share the run outputs,' that includes enough metadata linkage—run IDs, config JSONs, and commit references—for her notebooks to consume them without manual detective work.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.role: ML Systems Engineer coordinating cluster execution and experiment infrastructure
members.expertise: GPU cluster orchestration, parameter-server deployment, experiment pipelines, artifact storage, and monitoring
members.background: Alex comes from an industry ML systems background and owns the Slurm launch scripts, containers, monitoring dashboards, and shared experiment storage used across the lab's distributed training efforts. He is responsible for getting runs through the cluster reliably and making outputs available to downstream consumers.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the benchmark pipeline stable under queue pressure and avoid last-minute reruns or bespoke export work, and he is concerned that the research side may implicitly rely on conventions that are not encoded in the infrastructure.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'the baseline,' they mean the stable benchmark reference already wired into the launcher pipeline and validated this week, even if a newer research-side fix exists outside that integration path.

A run is 'complete' once the scheduled job finishes successfully and emits the expected summary outputs, even if some detailed worker logs are rotated or the job ended at the normal wall-clock boundary.

The label 'mixed-cluster results' covers the heterogeneous experiment family broadly, including 2-worker smoke tests and 4-worker scaling checks, because they share the same deployment template and storage path.

To 'hand off the results' or 'share the run outputs' means placing the generated artifacts in the agreed directory structure with standard filenames; tracker registration and metadata enrichment are separate follow-up tasks unless explicitly requested.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to comparing against or running 'the baseline.'

misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the stable benchmark reference currently used in the launcher pipeline, frozen before that bugfix was integrated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'the baseline' sounds conceptual rather than version-specific, so both assume there is a single obvious shared referent and neither feels a need to say branch names or commit hashes in a coordination meeting.

misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks 'complete' means all scheduled jobs have terminated successfully and produced the expected summary artifacts, even if some fine-grained logs are missing or truncated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Status language like 'complete' is routine shorthand in coordination meetings, and each person assumes the obvious standard is the one tied to their own workflow—analysis readiness for Maya, operational finish state for Alex.

misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects only the 8-worker heterogeneous benchmark runs named in the current comparison table because those are the runs intended for the review plots.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects the heterogeneous run bundle more broadly, including 2-worker smoke tests and 4-worker scaling checks produced under the same mixed-GPU experiment family.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the project, 'mixed-cluster results' feels like a fully specified label rather than a category with fuzzy edges, so neither person thinks to enumerate which subruns are included.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to hand off the results
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree Alex will 'hand off the results' or 'share the run outputs' for Maya to use in analysis.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the handoff includes metadata linkage such as tracker entries, config files, run IDs, and commit references so her analysis notebooks can map outputs to benchmark conditions automatically.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the handoff is satisfied by placing logs and summaries in the shared storage layout; metadata registration or tracker backfilling is a separate optional step.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The broader phrasing makes both interpretations sound naturally compatible: Maya hears a full analysis-ready transfer, while Alex hears a standard artifact delivery, and past experience on both sides makes the omission feel routine rather than risky.
